lesson.title: When AI gets it wrong
lesson.subtitle: False alarms, misses, and what you can do

video.title: When AI gets it wrong
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — science teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Ms Amina Bello — teacher at the same school (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice, talking to the student (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: The message that went to spam
Who chooses, and why it goes wrong

scenes.visual: A dusty school pitch on a Friday afternoon. Half the team stands around in kit, waiting. Mr Okafor, whistle round his neck, scrolls his phone and finds the message in the spam folder: ‘Match moved to Saturday’. He holds it up, half laughing, half exasperated.
scenes.animation: The spam folder opens; the message highlights. Quick cut to the half-empty pitch.
scenes.narration: My phone put the message about our match in the spam folder. It said the match had moved to Saturday! Half our team turned up on Friday.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the course name, the lesson title and the AI track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how AI gets things wrong, and what you can do.

scenes.visual: Four messages, each with a bar showing its scam score: homework 10, match moved 62, free data 85, prize 94. A dashed line at 60 marks the threshold; everything above it slides into the spam folder, including the match message.
scenes.animation: Bars grow left to right; the dashed line draws across; the match message drops into spam.
scenes.narration: AI makes predictions, and predictions can be wrong. A spam filter gives every message a score: how scam-like does it look? Above a line, called the threshold, it goes to spam.

scenes.visual: Clean card with the AI chip, split in two. Left, ‘False alarm’: the harmless match message wrongly in spam. Right, ‘Miss’: a scam sitting in the inbox with no warning.
scenes.animation: Left half slides in, then the right; a warning icon pops on each.
scenes.narration: There are two kinds of mistake. A false alarm is when AI flags something harmless, like our match message. A miss is when something bad slips through, like a scam in your inbox.

scenes.visual: Two referees on a pitch. One blows the whistle at a light touch, and the players protest. The other waves play on while a clear foul happens behind him. A slider between them moves the line from strict to relaxed.
scenes.animation: Whistle lines pulse; the slider moves left and right.
scenes.narration: It’s like a referee. A strict one whistles at every touch, giving fouls that weren’t fouls: false alarms. A relaxed one lets real fouls go: misses. Move the line one way, and you get fewer of one mistake but more of the other.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor holds up his phone: ‘You have won a new phone! Claim your prize now’ sits in the inbox, no warning. Two answer cards drop in beside him.
scenes.animation: Mr Okafor slides in; answer cards drop with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A fake prize message lands in your inbox, and the filter says nothing. Which mistake is that?

scenes.visual: The ‘A miss’ card gets a check badge. The prize scam glows red in the inbox; beside it, the match message in spam is labelled ‘false alarm’ for contrast.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms); the two labels appear one after the other.
scenes.on_screen_text: A miss: the scam got through
scenes.narration: A miss: a real scam slipped through. A false alarm is the other way round: something harmless gets flagged, like my match message.

scenes.visual: A set of scales: on one side a hidden exam-date message, on the other a scam in the inbox. A group of people (a teacher, a parent, a student) move the threshold line together; the computer waits.
scenes.animation: The scales tip; the line moves as the people point.
scenes.narration: So where should the line go? It depends on which mistake hurts more, and people decide that, not the computer. For school messages, hiding a real one, like an exam date, may be worse than letting a scam through. Each job may need its own line.

scenes.visual: Three cards: voice typing turning a student’s sentence into nonsense, with sound waves from only a few speakers behind it; a translation app mixing up words of a local language; an empty slot in a stack of examples.
scenes.animation: Each card flips in; the empty slot pulses once.
scenes.on_screen_text: Gaps in the data cause mistakes
scenes.narration: Mistakes also come from gaps in the data. Voice typing that learned mostly from a few accents makes more mistakes with others. A translator that saw little of your language mixes up its words. That’s not your fault: the examples were missing.

scenes.visual: Three moves, one after another: a student opens the spam folder and checks a textbook; asks a teacher in the corridor; taps a ‘Not spam’ button on the phone.
scenes.animation: Each move slides in with its icon, about three seconds each.
scenes.narration: So what can you do? Check it: look in your spam folder, or compare with a trusted source. Ask a person: a teacher, a parent, a friend. And report it: many apps have a button to say “wrong” or “not spam”, and that helps fix it.

scenes.visual: The Darsi ‘Mistakes and thresholds’ lab on a phone: dots and squares along a score strip, a dashed threshold line, a slider, and a table counting caught, missed, false alarms and rightly quiet. The detector switches from ‘Smoke alarm’ to ‘Spam filter’.
scenes.animation: The threshold line slides; the counts in the table change; the switch flips.
scenes.narration: In the lab, you set the threshold for a smoke alarm, which must tell real smoke from cooking steam, then for a spam filter. Slide the line, and watch the counts change: caught, missed, false alarms. Then find where mistakes cost least, and notice it’s different for each job.

scenes.visual: Ms Amina in a school kitchen, pointing at a smoke alarm on the ceiling while a pot steams below it. Two answer cards appear beside her.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. For a smoke alarm, which mistake is worse?

scenes.visual: The ‘Missing a real fire’ card gets the check badge, then four summary lines and the takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Points arrive one by one, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Missing a real fire, so smoke alarms are set to go off easily. Remember: AI makes two kinds of mistake, false alarms and misses. People choose which matters more, and gaps in the data cause mistakes too. When AI gets it wrong: check, ask a person, report it.

scenes.visual: A student’s notebook page titled ‘AI mistake of the week’: a bad translation copied out, with ‘false alarm or miss?’ and ‘why?’ written underneath. Mr Okafor smiles beside it. End card: Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Lines write themselves in; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: this week, catch one AI mistake, like a wrong suggestion, a bad translation or a message in the wrong folder. Was it a false alarm or a miss? And what might have caused it?

checkpoints.prompt: A fake prize message lands in your inbox, and the filter says nothing. Which mistake is that?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a real scam slipped through without any warning: that’s a miss.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — nothing was flagged, and a real scam got through. That’s a miss. A false alarm flags something harmless.

checkpoints.prompt: For a smoke alarm, which mistake is worse?

options.text: A false alarm from cooking steam

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a missed fire can cost lives, so smoke alarms are set to go off easily.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a beep from steam is annoying, but a missed fire can cost lives. That’s why smoke alarms go off easily.
